metadata.title: Verifying Private AI Valuations

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali, and this is week one of the Private AI Valuation Agent. I asked Claude the question the whole project rests on. Then I went and checked the answer by hand, in real S E C filings. Here is what held up, and the two places my own plan broke.

show.event: Cream Claude composer, empty. Serif greeting 'Ola, HAI' + terracotta spark above it.
The ask types itself into the composer, character by character.
Send button arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'reading Form N-PORT…'.
Three output lines land in sequence — the ask arrives ANSWERED (COLD OPEN LAW).

props.command: Private AI companies have no public share price. Can mutual-fund disclosures give me one — and what would I have to verify by hand before I trust it?
output: funds file every holding: a dollar value AND a share count
divide one by the other → a price per share
verify by hand before you build the pipeline

beats.narration_text: Most of the AI industry's value sits in companies you cannot buy. OpenAI. Anthropic. Databricks. No ticker, no earnings call, no public price. But somebody is already writing a price down every quarter, and they have to show their work.

shot.visual_intent: The BLUF as kinetic type — the whole idea in one breath, no data, no exhibit (EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW).

show.event: Serif line 'Most of the AI industry's value sits in companies you cannot buy.' settles in.
OpenAI · Anthropic · Databricks land as three ink chips, one per spoken name.
Three ghosted labels — TICKER · EARNINGS CALL · PUBLIC PRICE — each struck through in ink as it is spoken.
Struck labels fade back; one terracotta line types in beneath: 'Somebody writes a price down every quarter.'

props.headline: Most of the AI industry's value sits in companies you cannot buy.
props.turn: Somebody writes a price down every quarter — and has to show their work.

beats.narration_text: Every mutual fund that owns a piece of one has to report it to the S E C. Form N-PORT. A dollar value, and a share count, position by position. Divide one by the other, and you get a price per share for a company that has no public price. That is the entire mechanism.

shot.visual_intent: A real N-PORT XML block; the two load-bearing tags lift out and perform the division that gives a private company a price.

show.event: An XML block fades up — the Anthropic position as filed, monospace ink on cream.
The <valUSD> tag highlights terracotta and lifts out of the block as the NUMERATOR slot.
The <balance> tag highlights and lifts out beneath it as the DENOMINATOR slot.
The two tags slide into a division: a rule draws between them, ÷ appears. Operands stay as TAG NAMES — no invented numerals (REBUILD LAW).
The quotient resolves to $259.14 in large serif — the one figure here that is confirmed (FACTCHECK rows 2 and 5, Fidelity/ARK).

props.caption: A price for a company that has no public price.

beats.narration_text: So I verified it by hand. Nineteen Anthropic positions, six fund families, read straight out of the filings. Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Alger and ARK all landed on the same price. Identical, to the cent. Then a new round repriced it, and BlackRock and Capital Group matched again, to four decimals, two days apart.

shot.visual_intent: The convergence chart, rebuilt native and animated: managers land on the line as they are named, then the dashed repricing jump draws on the spoken 'new round'.

show.event: Axes draw in — price scale left, four staggered filing dates along the bottom.
Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Alger, ARK each drop a terracotta dot onto the SAME horizontal line, one per spoken name.
The flat line joining them thickens and $259.14 sets large beside it — the point of the beat.
A dashed terracotta segment climbs steeply to the upper tier.
Two dots land on the new level; $589.0095 sets above them, '2 days apart' annotates between.

props.title: Six managers, one price — then a repricing
props.footnote: Anthropic PBC · 19 positions read by hand from Form N-PORT · staggered fiscal quarter-ends are what make propagation observable

beats.narration_text: Then my own plan broke. I had a filter that was supposed to isolate private holdings. It kept Fidelity and silently dropped the other five. No error, nothing to notice. Filers write N slash A, or nine zeros, for a missing identifier, and two of them flag restricted stock as unrestricted.

shot.visual_intent: The six managers enter whole; the filter sweeps and five fall out silently — the drop is the motion, not a label.

show.event: Six manager rows stand in ink, all equal weight; a thin terracotta filter bar sweeps down over them.
Fidelity's row gets a terracotta rule and the tag 'kept'.
The other five desaturate and slide right by a few pixels, tagged 'dropped' — one after another, no error badge anywhere.
An empty error console outline appears beneath and stays empty — the silence made visible.

show.at: on 'N slash A, or nine zeros'
show.event: Two cause chips type in: "N/A" and "000000000", then a third: 'restricted flagged unrestricted ×2'.

props.title: The filter dropped five of six managers — silently

beats.narration_text: Second break. The plan expected a few thousand private rows a quarter. The real number was six hundred and six thousand. So I inverted the pipeline. Match companies by name first, confirm they are private second. That shrank the hardest part of this project by about six hundred times.

shot.visual_intent: The magnitude error enacts itself — the planned bar is dwarfed as the real bar grows on the spoken number; then the two pipeline stages physically swap order.

show.event: A short ink bar draws to ~3,000 rows and labels itself 'planned'.
The terracotta 'actual' bar grows across the full frame while a counter races to 606,028 — it lands on the spoken figure.
Beat of stillness; caption '11.3% of every holding row filed' sets under the big bar.
Two stage blocks — MATCH BY NAME and CONFIRM PRIVATE — visibly swap positions along the arrow.
The big bar collapses down to the small one; '606,028 → ~1,000 per quarter' sets in terracotta.

props.title: The real number was 606,028 rows a quarter
props.actualCaption: per quarter — 11.3% of every holding row filed
props.measuredNote: Measured across all 5,347,869 holding rows in the 2026 Q2 SEC bulk data set

beats.narration_text: So, the output for week one. The approach is proven: the S E C's bulk data matched my hand read filings, fifteen out of fifteen. Universe version one is frozen at six companies. SpaceX went in. Cohere came out, because every single Cohere match turned out to be Coherent Corp, a public optics company.

shot.visual_intent: The frozen universe, rebuilt as a growing bar chart with a coverage floor — and the subtraction (Cohere) is the beat's last, biggest move.

show.event: A 15/15 match counter ticks up to full and stamps 'exact, 0 mismatches'.
Six terracotta bars grow in rank order — Databricks 152, Anthropic 84, OpenAI 73, SpaceX 69, Anduril 50, Cerebras 28 — a dashed 'coverage floor' rule under them.
SpaceX's bar pulses once and picks up the note 'added — was not in the plan'.
A greyed Cohere row slides in below the floor and is struck through.
The callout resolves: 'all 1,094 matching rows are Coherent Corp — a public optics company'.

props.title: Universe v1, frozen on measured coverage
props.subtitle: Distinct fund filings holding each company, 2026 Q2

included.label: SpaceX
included.note: added — was not in the plan

included.label: Cerebras
included.note: kept — it went public, a free accuracy check

props.removedTitle: Cohere was removed — it was never there.
removedLines: All 1,094 matching rows are Coherent Corp, a public optics company.
A name match alone would have invented an entire price series.

beats.narration_text: Week one on one page. The mechanism works, and anyone can check it. My own plan was wrong in two places, and both defects turned up by hand, before a single line of pipeline code. Universe version one is frozen at six. Next week: eight quarters into the database, then entity resolution.

show.event: The Claude artifact page opens — 'Week 1 — one page' in serif.
Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause, the last one terracotta.

artifactLines: Mechanism: value ÷ share count on Form N-PORT gives a private company a price — and anyone can re-read the filing.
Verified by hand: 19 Anthropic positions, 6 fund families. Four managers agreed to the cent; two more matched to four decimals after a repricing.
Defect 1 — my filter dropped 5 of 6 managers silently, on missing-identifier conventions the plan never anticipated.
Defect 2 — 606,028 private rows a quarter, not a few thousand. Inverting the pipeline shrank it ~600x.
Universe v1 frozen at 6 — SpaceX in, Cohere out. Next: 8 quarters loaded, then entity resolution.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Pick a private company you think a mutual fund owns, find its most recent Form N-PORT on EDGAR, pull the reported value and the share count for that position, divide them, and then ask what would have to be true for that number to be wrong. That last clause is the whole point. The division takes a second. Deciding whether to trust it is the actual work, and it is exactly where my plan broke, twice.

show.event: Composer returns, greeting reads 'Your turn.' — the one greeting that drops the persona.
The suggested prompt types itself in as the narration reads it aloud, verbatim.
Running text reads 'paste this into Claude…'; the send button holds armed while the narration discusses what to look for.
